The insidious part is that this failure mode is nearly invisible in standard evaluation, because the same miscalibrated PM used for training is typically reused for validation, creating a closed epistemic loop where hacking behavior looks like policy improvement. A topological framing matters here because the exploitable regions aren't random — they form connected low-loss manifolds in output space, meaning a sufficiently expressive policy can find and ride these manifolds through gradient descent without ever triggering obvious distributional alarms.

Contrastive pretraining (as in embedding models or CLIP-style objectives) produces the most aggressively clustered geometry — representations collapse toward coarse semantic equivalence classes — which makes the smoothness prior very flat within a semantic cluster and very steep across clusters; reward hacking under this prior would concentrate in inter-cluster boundary regions where the PM must interpolate across a steep gradient, producing high-confidence but poorly grounded scores for outputs that straddle semantic categories. The practical implication, not yet systematically studied, is that PM ensembles built from models with different pretraining objectives would have genuinely decorrelated extrapolation geometries — a causal LM and a contrastive model would fill coverage voids along orthogonal dimensions — making their disagreement a much stronger epistemic uncertainty signal than same-objective ensembles; the absence of this in current RLHF practice (nearly all PMs are causal LM fine-tunes) is a structural blind spot.
